To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of perfusion CT in combination with 18F-FDG PET-CT for the assessment of colorectal cancer is feasible and reproducible.

(1) the metabolic-vascular parameters of primary colorectal tumors were significantly correlated with each other and (2) the inter- and intra-observer agreements of metabolic-vascular parameters were significantly improved when using an integrated (18)F-fluoro-2-deoxy-D-glucose (FDG) positron emission tomography (PET)/computed tomography (CT) scanner.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the effect of the inter- and intra-observer variability on the quantitative analysis of metabolic-vascular parameters of primary colorectal tumors by using integrated (18)F-fluorodeoxyglucose PET/CT and CT perfusion.

the effect of the inter- and intra-observer variation in the evaluation of primary colorectal cancers by using integrated 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-positron emission tomography and computed tomography (CT) and perfusion CT (pCT) on the metabolic and vascular tumor parameters.
a novel method for the analysis of the PET-CT and perfusion-CT data.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence is sufficient to conclude that there is an association between exposure to the chemicals in question and the health effect(s) discussed.
there is a significant correlation between the metabolic activity of the primary tumor and its vascularization, which can be measured with perfusion CT.

there are no clear indications for the use of PET/CT in the primary staging of colorectal cancer and in the follow-up of patients with colorectal cancer, but that the use of PET may be considered in selected patients with colorectal carcinoma.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

our study demonstrates that there is a strong correlation between the metabolic activity (SUVmax) and perfusion (CT perfusion) of primary colorectal tumors and that these parameters are reproducible and can be assessed in the same patients using integrated (18)F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET/computed tomography (CT) and perfusion CT.
the authors have demonstrated that the interobserver variability in the measurement of metabolic parameters is high, and that the intraobserver variability is also high, but less so.

we have shown that the use of PET/CT and CT perfusion can provide additional information on the biology of colorectal cancer and that this information can be integrated with morphological information to improve the diagnostic accuracy of PET/CT.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can use the information about a person's metabolism to predict their response to chemotherapy.
we need to do more to understand how the gut microbiota is involved in the development of cancer.
we can now measure tumor hypoxia and tumor metabolism using a single tracer, 18F-fluoride.
